1: If you think buddhi is superior to action, Janārdana, then why are you setting me to this terrible action, Keśava?
2: Your words seem mixed, and they seem to bewilder my buddhi. Decide, and tell me the one thing by which I may reach what is better.
3: I declared before now, sinless one, that there are two ways of standing firm in this world: for the followers of sāṅkhya, the yoga of knowledge, and for the yogīs, the yoga of action.
4: A person does not reach actionlessness by not starting on actions, and does not come to perfection by renouncing alone.
5: For no one ever stays without acting, even for a moment. Everyone is made to act, with no choice in it, by the guṇas born of nature.
6: Whoever sits with the organs of action held in check, while the mind keeps remembering the objects of the senses, has a deluded self, and that person's conduct is called false.
7: But whoever controls the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and takes up the yoga of action with the organs of action, unattached, is the one who excels.
8: So do the action prescribed for you, for action is superior to not acting. Without action you could not even keep your body going.
9: Apart from action done for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action. Perform action for that purpose, son of Kuntī, free of attachment.
10: Long ago the lord of creatures created creatures together with sacrifice, and said: by this you shall bring forth. Let this be yours, and let it yield, like milk, the desires you wish for.
11: Nourish the gods by this, and let those gods nourish you. Nourishing one another, you will attain the highest good.
12: For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you wish for. Whoever enjoys what the gods have given without giving to the gods is nothing but a thief.
13: The good, who eat what is left of the sacrifice, are freed from all faults. But the wicked, who cook only for themselves, eat sin.
14: Beings come from food, and food arises from rain. Rain comes from sacrifice, and sacrifice arises from action.
15: Know that action arises from brahman, and that brahman arises from the imperishable. Therefore the all-pervading brahman is always established in sacrifice.
16: The wheel has been set turning in this way. Whoever here does not keep it turning, whose life is sin and whose delight is the senses, lives in vain, son of Pṛthā.
17: But for the human being whose delight is in the self alone, who is satisfied by the self and content in the self alone, there is nothing that has to be done.
18: Such a person has no purpose at all here in what is done, nor in what is left undone, and does not depend on any being for any purpose.
19: Therefore always perform the action that is to be done, unattached. For a person who acts unattached reaches the highest.
20: For it was by action alone that Janaka and the others attained perfection. Even if you look only to the holding together of the world, you ought to act.
21: Whatever the best person does, others do the very same. The standard that person sets, the world follows.
22: For me, son of Pṛthā, there is nothing at all to be done in the three worlds, and nothing unattained that I have yet to attain. And still I am engaged in action.
23: For suppose I were ever to stop engaging tirelessly in action, son of Pṛthā, when people follow my path in every way.
24: These worlds would sink into ruin if I did not act. I would be the maker of confusion, and I would destroy these creatures.
25: As the unknowing act, attached to their action, descendant of Bharata, so should the knowing one act, unattached, wishing to bring about the holding together of the world.
26: One should not split the buddhi of the unknowing, who are attached to action. The knowing one, disciplined, should perform all actions and so lead them to delight in all actions.
27: Actions are being done, in every way, by the guṇas of nature. One whose self is deluded by the sense of I thinks: I am the doer.
28: But the one who knows the truth, mighty-armed one, about the two divisions, of guṇa and of action, thinks: the guṇas are moving among the guṇas. And so that one is not attached.
29: Those deluded by the guṇas of nature are attached to the actions of the guṇas. The one who knows the whole should not unsettle those slow ones who do not know the whole.
30: Lay down all actions in me, with your mind on the self. Become free of wishes and free of the sense of mine, and fight, with your fever gone.
31: Those humans who always follow this teaching of mine, with faith and without finding fault, are freed from actions too.
32: But those who find fault with this and do not follow my teaching, know them to be deluded in all knowledge, lost and without understanding.
33: Even one who has knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature. Beings go the way of nature. What will restraint do?
34: Attraction and aversion are settled in the object of each sense. One should not come under the power of these two, for they are the robbers on one's road.
35: One's own dharma, though without merit, is better than another's dharma well performed. Death in one's own dharma is better. Another's dharma brings fear.
36: Then what is it, descendant of Vṛṣṇi, that drives a person to do evil, even without wishing to, as if set to it by force?
37: It is desire, it is anger, arising from the guṇa of rajas, a great devourer and a great evil. Know this as the enemy here.
38: As fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror by dust, as an embryo is covered by its membrane, so this is covered by that.
39: Knowledge is covered by this, the constant enemy of the one who knows, son of Kuntī, which has the form of desire and is a fire that is hard to fill.
40: The senses, the mind and the buddhi are said to be its seat. Through these it covers knowledge and deludes the embodied one.
41: Therefore, bull of the Bharatas, restrain the senses first, and then strike down this evil one, the destroyer of knowledge and discernment.
42: They say the senses are higher. Higher than the senses is the mind, but higher than the mind is the buddhi. And the one who is beyond the buddhi, that is he.
43: So, knowing what is higher than the buddhi, and steadying the self by the self, strike down the enemy, mighty-armed one, who has the form of desire and is hard to approach.
